accounts.signUp: Open public sign-up: anyone who reaches the site can register (email check, Google sign-in), like Higgsfield. The owner's words: open public sign-up. Keep the other modes (invite-only, owner-approved, closed) as settings the owner can pick, but open sign-up must be a first-class, fully built path (verification, abuse controls, per-person limits). Plans, credits and payments ARE in scope for the Platform mode (see deploymentModes). The mode is chosen in the first-run setup (see 'setup').
accounts.libraries: Own library each AND teams: every account has its own private Library, projects, characters and history. People can also join a team (or several); inside a team they share with the team (team library/folders/projects/characters/brand kits/LoRAs, shared on purpose or created in the team space), on top of sharing with a person or as a public link. The owner's words: 'Own library each as well as teams features to share within the same team if users join a team'.
accounts.localUse: Ask on first launch: the first screen offers 'Create your account' or 'Just me on this computer' (no sign-in, local addresses only, as today); switchable later in Settings.
accounts.paidKeys: Both, all configurable from setup (the owner's words: 'Both features, all configurable from setup'). Support the owner's keys paying for others with a per-person monthly limit and per-person spend shown to the owner, AND each person adding their own keys which then pay for their work. The owner chooses in the first-run setup (and later in Settings) which applies: owner's keys with limits, own keys required, or both (own keys first, owner's keys within the limit).
accounts.enterprise: Enterprise-level features as well (the owner's words: 'enterprise level features as well'): e.g. team roles and permissions, admin console, SSO (OIDC and SAML), SCIM provisioning, verified domains / auto-join, enforced 2FA and session policies, audit log, per-team and per-member spend limits and usage reports, team keys, seat management, data export and deletion, retention. Plan them all; order packages so the core (accounts, own libraries, teams, sharing) lands first and enterprise features follow.
accounts.setup: Sign-up related choices are asked during the first-run setup too (the owner's words: 'Sign up related stuff as well can be asked during setup'), alongside the paid-keys choice. The setup wizard (after 'Create your account', for the owner) asks, with sensible defaults preselected and everything changeable later in Settings: who can sign up (open / owner-approved / invite-only / closed; the owner's own answer here was open), email verification on/off and how email is sent (SMTP or none, with what happens without email), sign-in methods to offer (email + password, passkeys, Google / GitHub / any OIDC with their client ids), allowed or blocked email domains, whether people may create teams, the paid-keys mode and the default monthly limit per person, and the public site address. Skippable: 'Just me on this computer' skips all of it.
accounts.deploymentModes: THREE ways to run Fuobe, all designed and crafted well, chosen in the first-run setup (the owner's words: 'It can be just for their own use - single access to configure everything themselves or as a host for their in house studio or setup as a platform to offer like higgsfield does- to the public with an admin panel that controls the whole thing and users get access with a plan. Do all three designs done and crafted well'). (1) PERSONAL: one person, single access, configures everything themselves (today's Fuobe; optional sign-in for reaching it remotely; 'Just me on this computer' is this mode with no sign-in). (2) IN-HOUSE STUDIO: a company or studio hosts Fuobe for its own people: accounts, own libraries, teams and sharing within teams, enterprise features (SSO, SCIM, audit log, roles, policies, spend limits and usage per team/member, team keys). (3) PLATFORM: a public service like Higgsfield: open sign-up, users get access with a PLAN (subscription plans and credits, top-ups, payments), an ADMIN PANEL that controls the whole thing (users, plans and prices, credits, which models and features each plan gets, per-model credit prices over the operator's cost, moderation and abuse, announcements, analytics, settings). One codebase, one core; the mode decides what is on. A mode can be changed later (personal → studio → platform) without losing data.

accountsDropped.source: Summarised by the session that integrated PR #15 from the decision it was given; not the owner's own words.

engines: Owner, 10-30 (clarifies the 10-29 hosted-only rule): 'whatever is possible in cloud only in cloud, whatever possible in local can work on local. So it's not like if a particular lora isn't available in cloud, we remove it from local, no. If we can do lora only in local, then we do that on local, not remove it from both.' Each engine does everything it can. The cloud only uses models that are hosted (no substitute model), with what the hosted endpoint supports; the open engine keeps every capability it has (LoRAs, nodes, longer clips, references) even when the cloud can't match it. Never remove or weaken a local capability because the cloud lacks it; say plainly in the UI what each engine does.

ownerCalls_pr14.evolutionCloud: Move Evolution's cloud route from LTX-2.3 (a substitute model) onto fal's hosted Wan 2.2 Fun VACE, the same model as the GPU recipe, with what that endpoint supports; the GPU keeps its full recipe (references in the direction frames).
ownerCalls_pr14.speakName: Keep 'Fuobe Speak'. The GPU keeps the FusioniX LoRA; the cloud runs fal's InfiniteTalk without it; the UI says so.
ownerCalls_pr14.dopMixedMediaDefault: Keep Fuobe DoP as the default for DoP's 32 Mixed Media effects; the first evaluation run with paid keys does a blind comparison with Kling 2.5 Turbo, and the default goes back if Fuobe DoP clearly loses.
